examples: My sister has a really pretty face.
I wake up and wash my face in the morning.
I am embarrassed so my face is red.
nuance: 얼굴 means the whole face and is used for both looks and washing. For washing the face Koreans use 씻다, the same verb as for hands, not 감다.
mistakes: Using 감다 instead of 씻다 for washing the face

examples: My hair falls out a lot these days.
I cut my hair at the salon.
nuance: 머리카락 means the individual strands of hair, while 머리 can mean both head and hair. Use 머리카락 when you want to be clear you mean the hair itself, not the head.

examples: I have a fever so my forehead is hot.
I bumped it so my forehead hurts.
nuance: 이마 is the forehead and Koreans often check it to feel for a fever. To say it feels hot use 뜨겁다, and to describe a wide forehead use 넓다, not 크다.
mistakes: Saying 이마가 커요 instead of 이마가 넓어요

examples: It is cold so my cheeks are red.
nuance: 볼 means the cheek and is often used to describe chubby or rosy cheeks. The word 뺨 also means cheek but sounds harsher and links to slapping, so 볼 is gentler in daily talk.
mistakes: Using 뺨 when 볼 sounds more natural and gentle

examples: I chewed too much so my jaw hurts.
I sit resting my chin on my hand.
The model has a pointy chin.
nuance: 턱 means both the chin and the jaw, so context decides which one. For jaw pain from chewing Koreans say 턱이 아프다, and resting the chin on a hand uses the verb 괴다.
mistakes: Thinking 턱 only means chin and not the whole jaw

examples: I sat long so my shoulder hurts.
I used the computer a lot so my shoulder is stiff.
nuance: 어깨가 아프다 is a very common complaint after sitting or working too long. For a stiff shoulder Koreans say 어깨가 결리다 with 결리다, a special verb for muscle stiffness.
mistakes: Saying 어깨가 딱딱해요 instead of 어깨가 결려요 for stiffness

examples: I carried a heavy bag so my arm hurts.
I fell and hurt my arm.
nuance: 팔 is the whole arm and is often the object of actions like raising or injuring. To raise the arm use 팔을 들다, and to hurt it use 팔을 다치다 with the object particle.
mistakes: Saying 팔을 올리다 when 팔을 들다 is more natural

examples: I caught it in the door so my finger hurts.
I cut my finger with a knife.
nuance: 손가락 means finger and is part of the hand 손. For cutting a finger Koreans use 베다, a special verb for slicing cuts, not the general 다치다 only.
mistakes: Saying 손가락을 잘랐어요, which sounds like cutting it off

examples: I climbed many stairs so my knee hurts.
I fell and hurt my knee.
My knee is swollen so I cannot walk well.
nuance: 무릎이 아프다 is common for older people or after climbing stairs. To kneel down Koreans say 무릎을 꿇다 with the special verb 꿇다, which is used only for kneeling.
mistakes: Saying 무릎을 앉다 instead of 무릎을 꿇다 for kneeling

examples: I lay down too long so my back hurts.
It is itchy so I scratch my back.
I stand leaning my back on the wall.
nuance: 등 is the upper back, while 허리 is the lower back or waist, so Koreans separate them. For an itchy back use 등을 긁다 with 긁다, the verb for scratching.
mistakes: Using 등 when you mean the lower back 허리

examples: I ran up stairs so my chest hurts.
I am nervous so my heart races.
I feel stifled so my chest aches.
nuance: 가슴 means the chest and also stands for the heart in feelings. So 가슴이 아프다 can mean physical chest pain or emotional heartache, and context tells you which one.
mistakes: Thinking 가슴이 아프다 only means physical pain

examples: I sat all day so my lower back hurts.
I hurt my lower back lifting something heavy.
Straighten your back and sit properly.
nuance: 허리 means both the waist and the lower back, so 허리가 아프다 usually means lower back pain. This is one of the most common complaints, and to sit up straight you say 허리를 펴다.
mistakes: Using 등 instead of 허리 for lower back pain
